AI-related debt binge may pressure European bond markets

Nov 3 : Europe's bond markets face a fresh headwind as US technology companies increasingly tap European investors to finance AI spending, boosting corporate debt supply and potentially lifting borrowing costs for other firms and governments. While tech-related borrowing in Europe has lagged the United States, investors say that leaves scope for a larger wave of issuance across euro, sterling and Swiss franc markets in coming months. Alphabet launched its second euro-denominated bond sale this year on Monday, following a €9 billion ($10 billion) issue in May. Investors expect other so-called hyperscalers — or Big Tech companies — including Meta, Amazon and Microsoft, to increase borrowing outside the US as they fund large-scale AI infrastructure investments.

"Europe has been behind the US in terms of issuance in the tech space but the activity is accelerating," said Marion Le Morhedec, chief investment officer for fixed income at Fidelity International. She estimates that €40 billion to €60 billion of issuance is in the pipeline. Issuing debt in foreign currencies also allows companies to hedge the currency risk from their global assets, while taking advantage of relatively lower borrowing costs in markets like Europe. Europe's deep capital markets offer an attractive source of funding. But while greater issuance expands the pool of highly rated corporate debt available to investors, it could also raise borrowing costs for European companies and governments already grappling with fiscal and inflation concerns. TECH BORROWING ACCELERATES IN EUROPE US markets have absorbed more than $250 billion of technology-related debt issuance so far this year, up 81 per cent from the same period last year. In Europe, issuance totals $39.3 billion, up about 5 per cent year-on-year, LSEG data shows. Despite investor concerns over whether Big Tech's massive AI investments will deliver returns quickly enough — spurring a selloff which erased more than $2 trillion from the tech-heavy Nasdaq's market value last month — analysts and investors expect bond issuance to remain strong. BNP Paribas expects euro-denominated investment-grade corporate bond net supply to rise 83 per cent to €192 billion ($214 billion) in 2027, up from €105 billion this year. Offshore bond issuance by US companies — dubbed the "reverse Yankee" in reference to Yankee bonds — is forecast to account for around €80 billion to €90 billion of the 2027 total debt supply, with hyperscalers making up the bulk of that, said Giulio Baratta, global co-head of investment grade finance at BNP Paribas. "It is undeniable that if any of these hyperscalers go into the market with a multi-billion deal to execute in a day, everybody knows about it and everybody needs to pay attention," said Baratta, who helped arrange Alphabet's May euro bond sale. JUMBO DEALS COULD TEST DEMAND The influx of debt could widen investment-grade credit spreads as hyperscalers compete with other highly rated borrowers across sectors such as utilities, telecommunications and automakers for investor demand. Asset swap spreads on the ICE BofA Euro Investment Grade index widened by 11 basis points last month, suggesting investors are demanding greater compensation to hold corporate bonds relative to interest-rate swaps. Issuers may need to offer pricing concessions to secure sufficient demand as supply expands, analysts say, potentially raising funding costs for other companies. Investors in European markets also have less experience absorbing the multitranche transactions that have become commonplace in the US. Such deals could therefore temporarily widen European investment-grade credit spreads, said Jonathan Owen, a member of TwentyFour Asset Management's multi-sector bond portfolio management team. SOME EUROPEAN ISSUERS SHIFT TO SHORTER MATURITIES Strong investor demand has so far absorbed the supply. But a series of jumbo deals of €10 billion to €20 billion could test that appetite, particularly if several issuers come to market simultaneously, analysts said. Some European companies are already responding to volatile long-term yields and expectations of heavier issuance by favouring shorter maturities, investors say. "We definitely observe that corporate, non-hyperscaler corporate issuers are staying away from the long end," said Vontobel portfolio manager Christian Hantel, without naming specific companies. "What has been a normal 10-year maturity bond, now they move to five to seven years." The additional issuance could further weigh on government bond markets, which are already under pressure from investor worries about fiscal and inflation risks. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said last week that debt issuance by hyperscalers had contributed to rising sovereign bond yields. "People are very much focused on the amount of AI supply that we're getting at the long end and what that means for government bonds," Owen said, adding that hyperscaler debt offers high credit quality while typically yielding more than government bonds. ($1 = 0.8948 euros)

Source: Reuters

FAST

HONG KONG, Nov 3 : Tech companies will need to raise more capital to help meet the enormous demand for the AI industry's growth boom, but there is a risk of an industry correction, global financial leaders said on Tuesday. Tech stocks globally have faced pressure in recent weeks as growing concerns about AI spending trigger a new wave of selloffs, with combined spending set to exceed $730 billion this year, up from about $700 billion. Most of the major tech companies were expected to raise more capital to keep up with the enormous likely demand from the AI industry's growth, said Jon Gray, president of Blackstone, which is an active investor in AI infrastructure. "Now you're in an environment where the demand's running well ahead of supply," Gray said at an investment gathering in Hong Kong, citing "pretty extraordinary" demand for computing power.

"So that gives me a lot of comfort," he added. "Meta and Google and Oracle raising equity ... SpaceX going public, Anthropic going public," Gray said. "On top of it ... the data centers, the energy needs are enormous." STRONG COMPANIES WITH 'GOOD STORIES' Despite some AI-related market upheavals, strong companies with "good stories" would still be able to raise capital, though the industry's strong growth could create volatility for investors, said Goldman Sachs Chief Executive David Solomon. "But things will go wrong too, and we'll get things wrong," he added at the event, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit. "Investors will find situations where they pick wrong, where they lose money ... It's important to have a balanced, diversified view." JPMorgan Vice Chairman Daniel Pinto said he was bullish on AI, but the market was pricing in revenue and earnings growth for related companies that was too steep. "I do believe that it has a positive, slow curve and it may not be as steep as the market is pricing," he said. "So I think that it could be a correction in the AI sector," he said, adding that other firms with high valuations related to AI could come under pressure as the industry started to recalibrate its expectations. Last month, S&P said it expected the top six US hyperscalers - Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Oracle, Meta and SpaceX - to spend more than $7 trillion on data centers and other AI-related capex between 2025 and 2030, while having negative free cash flow until at least next year. Citadel Securities Chief Executive Peng Zhao said the sheer scale of capital and growth in AI was proving difficult for some investors to value correctly, which was adding to volatility in the sector. "Our ability to really know what this technology will do and its revenue potential is very, very limited due to the fact that we've never seen anything like this," he said. "It's not so much that people all of a sudden develop a bearish view of what the technology can accomplish, but it's rather the sudden realization that we can only know so much ... the numbers involved are so huge." Morgan Stanley Chief Executive Ted Pick flagged emerging early signs of US markets edging close to a correction, with a majority of stocks in major indices off nearly 10 per cent. The latest test of investor appetite is a sale of €6 billion ($6.7 billion) in bonds on Monday by Google parent Alphabet. ASIA-PAC TECH FUNDRAISING MORE THAN TRIPLED Fundraising by Asia-Pacific tech companies more than tripled to $125.8 billion in the first three quarters of 2026 from $36 billion a year earlier. The growth was driven by a wave of semiconductor and AI-related deals, such as Chinese chipmaker CXMT’s $9.8-billion IPO and Enflame Technology's $910.6-million listing, LSEG data shows. Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta have signalled that spending on AI will not slow. In one of the largest debt deals tied to the AI buildout, Blackstone agreed last week to provide financing of $63 billion with Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic. The rising cost of capital and some of today's scepticism will slow the pace, however, Gray added. "But the overall trend is towards greater investment and therefore more needs for multiple forms of capital." Emmanuel Roman, CEO of asset manager PIMCO, said AI financing deals are attractive, with more coming for the firm.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 3 : Australia's largest pension fund, the A$430 billion ($301.7 billion) AustralianSuper, said it will stick to the "picks and shovels" of the AI industry as it navigates unprecedented turbulence in the market for global tech stocks.  Mark Hargraves, the head of AustralianSuper's international equities and private equity business, said the fund believed chipmakers and hyperscaler data centres would weather the current storm engulfing the AI sector. The comments show how one of Australia's biggest investors is positioning its AI holdings as doubts grow over whether the sector's earnings can justify its astronomical valuations.  One of the Melbourne-based firm's largest AI-linked exposures in its balanced portfolio is Nvidia, where it holds about A$3.05 billion worth of stock, according to recent filings. It holds more of the chipmaker's stock in other fund options.

AustralianSuper also owns about A$2.3 billion each in Microsoft and Alphabet, the filings show, as well as stakes in SK Hynix, SpaceX, Meta, Broadcom and Micron. "Large language models require compute power and the hyperscalers are providing that with the data centres, and that compute is driven by chips," Hargraves told Reuters in an interview on October 28.  "We've been quite focused on what we call the picks and shovels. But as the landscape is evolving, then we ... see the opportunity sets developing and we kind of move exposures accordingly." Globally, AI shares have stumbled amid growing doubts over whether earnings can keep pace with lofty valuations, prompting investors to reassess crowded positions after a prolonged rally. Still, many fund managers remain bullish on the sector's long-term prospects, betting demand for AI chips, data centres and related infrastructure has further to run. AI and AI-related stocks now made up about 40 per cent of the global equities market, Hargraves said, adding that the growth of the industry and its influence on markets had been the fastest emergence of a major investment theme he had seen in more than 30 years working in equities. "I've seen a lot of evolution over time. I think this cycle, the rate of evolution is happening faster than previous cycles," he said. "Some of the volatility you're seeing is reflective of that speed of change. It is leading things to change quite quickly and the best is having to constantly reassess things." Hargraves said that while AustralianSuper was a pre-IPO investor in Anthropic, he would not comment on the fund's intention in the upcoming share sale that would value the US company at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Instead, he said the IPO would give investors a greater insight into the financial forecasts of the large language models. ($1 = 1.4253 Australian dollars)

Source: Reuters

HONG KONG, Nov 3 : The dollar wavered alongside oil prices on Tuesday on hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran, while the Aussie was steady ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia's rate decision. Brent crude futures plunged more than 7 per cent on Monday in their sharpest single-day drop in months, after Tehran said its contacts with the US aimed at ending their eight-month war were continuing. Falling energy prices helped ease inflation concerns and dragged longer-dated US Treasury yields lower. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was steady at 4.9145 per cent, while that on the 30-year bond was also flat at 5.2868 per cent. Both had dipped to their lowest levels in nearly two months in the previous session.

The dollar index, which measures the currency against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, last traded a shade weaker at 101.76 after dropping to a one-month low on Monday. Meanwhile, an AI-driven stock market slump showed little sign of slowing down, hurting risk sentiment and lending some support to the dollar. Tensions around US midterm elections also loom large, helping to prop up the dollar as a safe-haven play. "Oil relief is growing, but conviction elsewhere remains thin," Sim Moh Siong, FX strategist at OCBC, said in a note. "Cheaper energy is reshaping FX dynamics, while AI concerns and US election risks reinforce our view that the USD remains supported." The euro was a touch higher at $1.1185 on the back of dollar weakness. The Japanese yen was flat at 157.915 per dollar during a local holiday. ANOTHER ROUND OF CENTRAL BANK MEETINGS Multiple central banks are scheduled to issue policy statements this week, including those in Britain, Australia, Norway and Sweden. The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise the official cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent on Tuesday, which would be the highest level since December 2008. The move would bring total tightening this year across five increases to 125 basis points. The Australian dollar was little changed at $0.7002. The kiwi was flat at $0.5617. Sterling strengthened 0.05 per cent to $1.3414 after PMI data showed British manufacturers started the final quarter of 2026 with the strongest output growth in more than two years. Economists polled by Reuters expect the Bank of England to raise its Bank Rate to 4.0 per cent from 3.75 per cent, the first hike since August 2023, when inflation was still more than triple its 2 per cent target.

BEIJING: Chinese regulators have rolled out a handful of measures, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets. Authorities also prodded index heavyweights and leading tech firms to try to stabilise their share prices, and are studying plans to ease margin rules to increase market liquidity. China's central bank and securities watchdog made their announcements on Monday (Nov 2) after the benchmark CSI300 Index slumped 8.5 per cent in October, its worst month since early 2016. Persistent weakness in the world's second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence.

Local media first reported that regulators had met with financial institutions on Monday to discuss tools to support capital markets. Share prices regained ground on Monday in expectation of supportive policies. As part of the measures, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) said on Monday it would conduct swap operations with financial institutions on Tuesday that could inject more than 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) into the stock market. It will be the third time the PBOC has used the liquidity tool, created two years ago to allow brokers, insurers and fund companies to obtain liquidity for stock purchases.

Related:

Has China’s AI bubble burst? What this means for the global tech boom

Tencent-backed Enflame triples in Shanghai debut as China AI chip bets surge

Commentary: China memory giant CXMT’s US$10 billion IPO is a flop

The PBOC also said a relending scheme designed to fund share buybacks and purchases would shift from a temporary arrangement to a long-term mechanism. The interest rate of the expanded scheme was cut to 1 per cent from 1.25 per cent. In a separate statement, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) urged key index constituents and "dragon head" tech companies to "actively buy back shares" and stabilize market value. The regulator will also prod some newly established exchange-traded funds to "speed up building stock positions", and encourage fund managers to buy shares in a down-cycle. The new round of PBOC swap operations "sends another strong signal of policymakers’ commitment to safeguarding capital market stability and supporting investor confidence", said Hao Zhou, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Guotai Haitong Securities. He said global volatility and external uncertainties continued to weigh on investor sentiment. The PBOC said bidding under the Securities, Funds and Insurance Companies Swap Facility would take place on Tuesday. It said 31 brokers and fund companies had already applied for swaps worth more than 100 billion yuan. The central bank previously conducted such operations in October 2024 and January 2025, injecting a combined 105 billion yuan into the market. The Shanghai Composite Index climbed 1.1 per cent on Monday, its biggest one-day percentage gain since Aug 27. The CSI300 and the Shanghai Composite Index both dropped roughly 1 per cent in early trade, giving up Monday's gains. “These measures were below expectations," said Chen Jiande, fund manager at Fujian Tianlang Asset Management Co. "Many investors in battered tech shares are taking advantage of any rebound to rush out." The tech-focused STAR Composite Index dropped 1.6 per cent. Investors also remain jittery over the financial health of state-owned developer Zhuhai Huafa Group, after media reported it was seeking extensions on some bank loans. Government bond yields held steady in early trade, with the 10-year and 30-year notes edging down about 0.3 basis points each.

SEOUL, Nov 3 : South Korea's headline inflation slowed in October, government data showed on Tuesday, providing a slight reprieve for central bankers but remaining firmly above target. Consumer prices rose 2.8 per cent year-on-year in October, down from a 2.9 per cent gain in September and nearly matching a 2.85 per cent increase forecast in a Reuters poll of economists. The consumer price index rose 0.2 per cent on a monthly basis after gaining 0.3 per cent in the previous month, the data showed. While the slower growth offers the Bank of Korea a brief respite, inflation remains well above its 2.0 per cent target. Amid elevated global energy prices and rising household borrowing, the BOK is widely expected to hike rates in the coming months, maintaining its tight monetary posture to calm persistent inflationary pressures in Asia’s fourth-largest economy. A separate poll showed consensus forecasts put the peak policy interest rate at 3.50 per cent, which prices in one more hike this November and another in the first quarter of 2027.

ORLANDO, Florida, Nov 2 : Oil prices tumbled on Monday on hopes that US-Iran peace talks could soon take place, which pushed bond yields around the world lower. Stock markets in Asia and Europe mostly benefited as a result, but the momentum evaporated in US hours, as investors turned their attention to Tuesday's midterm elections. In my column today, I look at the impact an AI-driven stock market rout could have on economic growth. It would vary from country to country, of course, but negative wealth effects and lower AI capex could stir recession fears across the developed world. Today's Key Reads • Investors gaming out Congress control for spending, AI outlook

• Sectors bracing for a pivot as US midterm elections loom • US Treasury auction changes loom in 2027; dealers eye long-end cuts • New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe • Manufacturing solid but strain of energy costs, supply disruptions starts to show • Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: South Korea +2 per cent, Japan -0.3 per cent. Europe +0.4 per cent, UK +0.3 per cent. Brazil -0.8 per cent, down every trading day since October 26 election. Nasdaq -1 per cent, S&P 500 -0.5 per cent, Dow +0.4 per cent.SECTORS/SHARES: Seven sectors on the S&P 500 rise, four fall. Consumer cyclicals +2 per cent, tech -2.7 per cent, energy -4 per cent. Apple trade choppy after results, Palantir +3 per cent. Alphabet slips again. Marvell -13 per cent, Lumentum -19 per cent after deal.FX: Dollar slips. Norwegian crown biggest G10 FX decliner, slumps more than 1 per cent. Swiss franc biggest G10 climber, +1 per cent. Chilean peso up nearly 2 per cent.BONDS: UK gilt yields -10 bps. US yields -4 bps at long end, curve flattens for the first day in four.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil -8 per cent, Brent's biggest fall since April. WTI's since July. Gold +2 per cent, still below $4,000. Today's Talking Points: Oil, election, & bluff? Crude oil prices had their biggest one-day fall in months on Monday, as hope spread that Iran may be more open to negotiations with the US to end the war. This comes on the eve of the US midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump's Republican Party is expected to fare badly, in large part because of the unpopularity of the war and the high energy prices it has caused. Could this wave of peace talk optimism finally be the one that is backed up with actual progress? Trump has previously signaled new attacks on Iran could follow the midterms, and he may face additional pressure from Israel to stay on the offensive. But on Monday he appeared to soften his stance, and said a deal "could happen". Things might become a little clearer after Tuesday's elections. At least, that's the hope. Cyber pass The AI trade has faltered recently mainly due to growing worries that companies are borrowing too much to fund a capex binge that might simply be too big. AI's potential existential threats to humanity have sparked intense debate, but these are risks that are almost impossible to price into asset values. In the same vein, cybersecurity risks are also difficult to quantify, but if AI increases the potential for cyberattacks, investors will have to prepare accordingly. And soon. Hackers stole more than $6 billion last week from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, prompting the exchange's customers to withdraw nearly $5 billion. The theft, potentially the largest-ever financial heist, underlines the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks. But it's not just crypto that's vulnerable. Hackers attacked fridges and freezers in supermarkets across Europe on Monday, forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar attack in France last month. Is AI a help or hindrance in the battle for cybersecurity? Central bank fest, part II After the Fed, ECB and BOJ last week, investors have another heavy dose of central bank policy decisions and guidance to absorb this week. The Reserve Bank of Australia kicks it off on Tuesday with an expected rate hike to 4.85 per cent, which would be its fifth this year. Decisions from Sweden, Poland, Brazil, Norway, the UK and Mexico follow. If there is a unifying theme, it is inflation, although price pressures aren't uniform. And nor is policymakers' reaction function — the RBA and Norges Bank have been hiking rates this year, while the BoE hasn't started yet. In Brazil, policymakers suddenly have to face a very different financial market environment following last month's presidential election. Watch out for some punchy FX moves this week, especially in the Brazilian real. FAST

SAN FRANCISCO : Apple warned on Monday (Nov 2) that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring gross margin for the crucial holiday quarter, but said it had taken steps to lock in supplies. Shares, little changed in after-hours trading after fiscal fourth-quarter results beat expectations, fell 4 per cent during a conference call after executives outlined the weaker outlook, but later pared losses to a 2 per cent decline. Early demand for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and higher prices boosted the quarter. Apple said it expects gross margin of 45 per cent to 46 per cent in the quarter ending in December, down from 47.9 per cent in the fourth quarter. It forecast services revenue growth of 8 per cent to 9 per cent, below analysts' expectations of 10.7 per cent. The results come as Apple experiments with a string of firsts under new CEO John Ternus, who took over in September. After nearly two decades of launching most new iPhones each autumn, Apple this year is spacing them out, with iPhone Pro and Duo models shipping this year and other models expected next year.

Apple also released a bevy of new non-iPhone products this quarter, including its first touchscreen laptops and first smart-home hub. The steady drumbeat of releases, analysts said, is meant to smooth out Apple's yearly revenue cycle, which for decades showed a huge holiday-quarter boom that petered out by late summer. Apple in recent weeks has grappled with customer reports of cracked screens on the iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, which sold out within hours online and spurred lines at stores last month. Fiscal fourth-quarter sales were US$114.48 billion, above analyst estimates of US$113.39 billion, according to LSEG data. Profit was US$2.10 per share, above estimates of US$1.99 even when excluding 5 cents from tariff refunds. IPHONE DUO SUPPLY CONSTRAINTS In an interview with Reuters, Ternus said "a very small percentage" of iPhone Duo units had been returned for display issues and that Apple is replacing them. He said the company is overall unable to meet demand, with no timeline for catching up. "Duo is constrained as of today," Ternus said. "The ramp is going well ... but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance." Fourth-quarter iPhone sales, which included iPhone 18 Pro models but not Duo, were US$57.58 billion, above estimates of US$56.54 billion, according to LSEG data. The staggered launch strategy comes as Apple faces headwinds from an AI-driven memory-chip price spike that could dampen the margin boost Apple derives from storage upgrades. "The big question for Apple moving forward will be how well they can weather the significant component price increases that have slowed their PC and smartphone competitors," said Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.  "The new iPhone Duo looks to be a big hit, but the company has to solve the screen glitches and ramp up its manufacturing output." PRICE RISES OFFSET CHIP COSTS As it launched the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple also raised iPhone 17 prices by US$100 and increased some MacBook prices, softening the blow of rising memory costs. "We did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which was partially offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components," Ternus said. "These price increases provided some offset." Fourth-quarter gross margins were 47.9 per cent, above estimates of 47.5 per cent, according to LSEG data. On the investor call, Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said Apple expects memory costs to keep rising into next year. Asked whether Apple had signed a long-term supply agreement, Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan did not directly confirm a deal but said Apple is working closely with memory suppliers and that its purchasing commitments increased by US$33 billion during the quarter. Shares of memory-chip maker Micron rose more than 1 per cent in after-hours trading on Monday, and shares of chip-manufacturing equipment makers KLA and Applied Materials also rose. Apple also pointed to Siri AI, which runs partially in Google's cloud, as a factor impacting margins. The company plans to charge more for iCloud+ subscriptions to offset AI costs, though it has not rolled out specific pricing. "There are going to be some usage limits on features that rely on server-side models, which include Siri AI and intelligent photo editing," Ternus said during the call. Mac sales were $10.79 billion, above estimates of US$9.61 billion. Services revenue was US$31.57 billion, in line with estimates of US$31.58 billion. iPad and wearables sales were US$6.23 billion and US$8.30 billion, both below estimates. Chinese sales were US$17.54 billion, below the US$18.58 billion analysts estimated, according to Visible Alpha data.

Source: Reuters/nh

Nov 2 : Scientists have discovered what they consider the strongest evidence yet of blood cells in a dinosaur fossil inside bone from the right leg of a medium-sized meat-eater that prowled Brazil some 115 million years ago during the Cretaceous Period. The researchers identified numerous microscopic structures in bone from the species Aratasaurus museunacionali that appear to be fossilized red blood cells. They also detected chemical evidence related to a key component of these cells — an iron-containing biomolecule called heme that is associated with hemoglobin, the protein that gives blood its red color. The evidence for blood cells and heme was found in vascular canals inside bones of an Aratasaurus individual, thought to be a juvenile or young adult about 4 years old when it died. The bipedal dinosaur would have measured about 10 feet (3.1 meters) long. "We have not found a vial of dinosaur blood. What we are seeing is a mineral and molecular echo of ancient biology, and that is scientifically much more interesting," said Kliti Grice, an organic and isotope geochemist at Curtin University in Perth, Australia, and lead author of the study published on Monday in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

"For me, the most surprising thing is that we can see the structures together with chemical evidence of their biological origin after such enormous geological time," Grice said. Red blood cells, continuously manufactured inside bone marrow, transport oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues and then help bring carbon dioxide back from the tissues to the lungs to be exhaled. Unlike hard bones and teeth, soft tissues like muscles and feathers are only rarely preserved in fossils. Cells present in bodily liquids like blood are even less commonly spotted in fossils. "Bones and teeth tell us an enormous amount about anatomy, growth and evolution. Molecular and cellular evidence potentially adds another level of biological information," Grice said. The research does not document dinosaur DNA, Grice said, cautioning against interpreting the discovery as evidence that intact dinosaur genetic material is present. "DNA and other large, information-rich biomolecules have very different preservation characteristics from small molecules and chemically transformed molecular remnants. The survival of cell-like morphology and heme-related chemical signals does not mean that the DNA that was originally contained within cells has survived," Grice said. 'TESTING THE LIMITS' The researchers also detected collagen-related amino acids in the Aratasaurus bone, though Grice noted that this is not equivalent to recovering an intact ancient protein or genetic information. Collagen is an abundant structural protein, sort of the scaffolding that holds the body's tissues together. "What the work does encourage us to do is keep testing the limits of molecular preservation rather than assuming that all biological information must disappear after a particular length of time," Grice said. The oldest-known DNA reported by scientists came from animals, plants and microbes dating to about 2 million years ago from sediment in Greenland. The Aratasaurus fossil was unearthed in a gypsum mine in Ceará state in northeastern Brazil, according to paleontologist and study co-author Alexander Kellner of the National Museum of Brazil. It includes parts of the right femur, tibia and foot. "What we believe is distinctive about the present study is the strength of the combined evidence: numerous red-blood-cell-like structures in situ within the dinosaur bone, their mineralization, their location in the vascular system, and associated in situ chemical evidence related to heme. To the best of our knowledge, that combination has not previously been demonstrated in a dinosaur fossil in this way," Grice said.

Source: Reuters

Nov 2 : Meta is eyeing at least $20 billion from a potential cross-border bond offering, Bloomberg News reported on Monday, with the tech giant tapping debt markets again to raise funds for its AI infrastructure build-out. Like many of its tech rivals, Meta has been raising funds through debt and equity to fund the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, though the heavy spending is now attracting heightened investor scrutiny. No final decision has been made and the potential debt offering's size may grow depending on investor demand, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The Facebook parent has asked Citigroup and Morgan Stanley to hold investor calls on Monday and Tuesday, the report added.

Meta, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Meta's potential dollar bond sale will span maturities of 5 to 30 years, while the euro offering will range from around 4 years to just over 38 years, Bloomberg News reported. The debt offering report comes about a week after the company announced plans for its largest-ever equity offerings of around $97.5 billion. The offerings include stock sales of about $37.5 billion it priced last week, and plans to later raise up to $60 billion through an at-the-market share-sale program. Meta had also raised $30 billion in a bond offering last year, and in April sold investment-grade bonds worth $25 billion. The heavy spending on AI infrastructure has weighed on Meta's cash flow, with the company reporting a cash burn of $2.12 billion in the third quarter. S&P Global Ratings on Friday revised its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable", citing significant uncertainty around the company's capital spending and free operating cash flow. Meanwhile, rival Alphabet is selling €6 billion ($6.72 billion) of bonds on Monday, according to a memo from one of the deal's managers. ($1 = 0.8924 euros)

Source: Reuters

Nov 2 : Snapchat parent Snap Inc has reached a settlement during a trial over claims brought by two teenagers who say the company designed the platform to be addictive, causing their depression, anxiety and eating disorders, attorneys for the plaintiffs said on Monday. Jury selection began last week for the trial, the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media after Snap, Meta Platforms, TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use. The plaintiffs had previously settled with Meta, TikTok and YouTube. "Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal," John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, trial attorneys for plaintiff K.D.B., said in a statement.

The trial was set to be the first for Snap in the sweeping litigation over social media's impact on teens, after the company settled the other cases that had been scheduled for trial. The company's chief executive, Evan Spiegel, had been expected to testify. The case had been selected from thousands of pending lawsuits as a bellwether intended to test the claims against Snap and the other companies and potentially influence how similar cases are resolved. The next bellwether trials are scheduled to begin in March, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers. A Snap spokesperson said in a statement that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts, and remains committed to “continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." Plaintiffs S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age 9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll.  The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make the apps safe places for young people to express themselves.  Social media companies face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts brought by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide.  In the first case to go to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube had been negligent and awarded a young woman $6 million in damages. The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the companies. The first school district chosen for trial settled with all of the companies. In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every state and US territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over claims its platforms harmed teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens. The deal conditioned $5 billion of the payout on the states reaching similar settlements with Snap, TikTok and YouTube.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 2 : A group representing nearly all major automakers on Monday urged US lawmakers to pass a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles when they return next week for a quick session after the midterm congressional elections. In September, the Senate sponsors of the bipartisan effort to ban Chinese vehicles agreed to delay an effort to fast-track the measure until November. "We need to protect the U.S. market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in American communities," said John Bozzella, who heads the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major automakers.

Source: Reuters
